metadata.title: HEURISTIC ANALYSIS OF THE NATIVE LANGUAGE CURRICULUM OF SUCCESSFUL COUNTRIES IN PISA AND TURKEY BY USING ANFIS

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study does not use student-level PISA microdata; instead, it performs document analysis of native language curricula from selected countries and correlates curriculum-derived counts (number of codes and learning outcomes) with published PISA 2018 reading scores. Because there is no student sampling frame or ILSA micro-dataset used, complex survey weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) and replicate weights are not applicable to the analysis as described. The analytic unit is the country/curriculum document, so population-representative weighting for students is not part of the modeling pipeline. The paper also does not report any weighting or stratification adjustments for the ANFIS modeling stage.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variable is the country-level PISA 2018 reading score (published summary), not a PV-based cognitive achievement outcome from ILSA microdata. Therefore, plausible values (PV1–PVn) are not generated or combined in this study. Missing-data handling is not reported because the analysis is based on document-derived counts and published PISA scores for a fixed set of countries, rather than on an individual-level dataset with item nonresponse requiring imputation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study selects nine countries: Singapore, Hong Kong, South Korea, Ireland, Finland, Canada, Sweden, the United States, and Turkey. Countries were chosen based on PISA reading performance across the 2012, 2015, and 2018 cycles (top-10 consistently successful or rising ranking in reading). For each country, the authors obtain the native language teaching program from official education ministries, then code the listening, speaking, reading, and writing skills and count (i) the number of learning outcomes and (ii) the number of codes/themes within each skill. The modeling uses these curriculum-derived counts as inputs and the published PISA 2018 reading scores as the output; no student-level inclusion/exclusion criteria are described.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (country-level scores) linked to native language curriculum documents (listening + reading)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading (country-level scores) linked to native language curriculum documents (listening + reading), the study leveraged the number of curriculum codes and learning outcomes for listening and reading to predict the PISA 2018 reading score, finding that the relationship was moderately strong with R² ≈ 0.78 and RMSE ≈ 20.57. This indicates that aligning native-language listening and reading learning outcomes/coding density may be associated with higher reading performance in PISA, though the analysis is correlational at the country/document level and does not establish causality.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (country-level scores) linked to native language curriculum documents (speaking + reading)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading (country-level scores) linked to native language curriculum documents (speaking + reading), the study leveraged the number of curriculum codes and learning outcomes for speaking and reading to predict the PISA 2018 reading score, finding that the relationship was stronger with R² ≈ 0.85 and RMSE ≈ 13.57. This indicates that emphasizing speaking-related learning outcomes alongside reading in native-language curricula may be more closely associated with PISA reading success than reading alone, while still remaining a non-causal, document-count-based heuristic.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (country-level scores) linked to native language curriculum documents (writing + reading)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading (country-level scores) linked to native language curriculum documents (writing + reading), the study leveraged the number of curriculum codes and learning outcomes for writing and reading to predict the PISA 2018 reading score, finding that the relationship was strong with R² ≈ 0.84 and the lowest RMSE ≈ 8.78 among the four models. This indicates that strengthening writing-related learning outcomes/coding density together with reading may be associated with higher PISA reading performance, though the evidence remains heuristic and based on curriculum document counts rather than student achievement PVs.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (country-level scores) linked to native language curriculum documents (listening + speaking + reading + writing)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Model 4 (integrated listening + speaking + reading + writing): RMSE = 17.3951; R² = 0.683623
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading (country-level scores) linked to native language curriculum documents (listening + speaking + reading + writing), the study leveraged the number of curriculum codes and learning outcomes across all four language skills to predict the PISA 2018 reading score, finding that the relationship weakened with R² ≈ 0.68 and RMSE ≈ 17.40. This indicates that simply expanding/combining all language-skill learning outcomes in the curriculum may not translate into stronger association with PISA reading success, suggesting the need for targeted curriculum design rather than maximal coverage.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses an ANFIS (Adaptive Neuro-Fuzzy Inference System) approach to relate native language curriculum content to PISA reading performance at the country level. For nine countries (Singapore, Hong Kong, South Korea, Ireland, Finland, Canada, Sweden, the United States, and Turkey), the authors extract document-based counts for listening, speaking, reading, and writing: the number of learning outcomes and the number of codes/themes within each skill. These counts are used as ANFIS inputs, while the output is the published PISA 2018 reading score. Four ANFIS models are estimated: reading+listening (R²=0.7807, RMSE=20.5737), reading+speaking (R²=0.8517, RMSE=13.5731), reading+writing (R²=0.8447, RMSE=8.7802), and all four skills combined (R²=0.6836, RMSE=17.3951). The strongest fit occurs for reading+speaking and reading+writing, while the integrated model shows weaker association; however, the analysis is heuristic and correlational at the curriculum/document level, with no student-level PVs or survey-weighted inference.
